pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Speed and energy

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England):** there is NO general 'energy' topic at KS2 — energy enters at KS3 — so there is no direct UK primary statutory match; the nearest UK home for the reasoning is the KS2 'Working scientifically' skills (using evidence/observations to construct explanations) and forces work on what changes an object's motion.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** 4-PS3-1 (verbatim) '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-1]'; DCI PS3.A '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-1]'; assessment boundary excludes quantitative speed measures and any precise/quantitative definition of energy. This topic is therefore NGSS-anchored.

- **Operational details:** Strictly qualitative: more speed → more effect (more damage, pushes things farther, louder bang), and the name 'kinetic energy' / 'energy of motion'. NO formulas, no ½mv², no quantitative speed measures — the win is an evidence-based explanation, not a calculation. It sits on 'Naming types of energy' (kinetic vocabulary) and feeds collisions and, later, the KS3 kinetic energy store.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, age 9-10) — children use evidence to build the explanation that a moving object has energy and that the faster it moves the more energy it has.
bestPractices: Build the idea from evidence the child gathers: roll a ball at different speeds into a row of skittles / a sand pit / a block and have them observe that the faster ball knocks over more, pushes farther, makes a bigger dent — 'more speed, more effect' IS the evidence for 'more energy'.
Control the variable: use the SAME object so only speed changes; this both isolates speed and quietly models fair testing (mass effects are a separate, later idea).
Name it precisely — 'kinetic energy' or 'energy of motion' — and tie the word to the observation, so the term labels a thing they've seen, not an abstraction.
Keep it qualitative and comparative ('faster → more', 'slower → less'); the assessment boundary explicitly excludes measuring speed or quantifying energy at this age.
Distinguish energy from force/speed in talk: the fast ball HAS more energy (shown by what it can do), rather than 'carries a force' — heading off the impetus idea that a moving thing contains a push.
keyRepresentations: A launch-and-hit set-up: same ball at low/medium/high speed into skittles or a block, with the result (how far / how many) as the visible evidence.
A simple 'energy meter' or bar that grows as the chosen speed increases — linking speed to amount of kinetic energy.
A comparison strip: slow vs fast trial side by side with their outcomes, for 'which had more energy, and how do you know?'.
Everyday anchors: a gentle vs hard kick of a football; a slow vs fast bumper car; wind turbines spinning faster in stronger wind.
commonMisconceptions: 'Only living things / engines have energy' — a rolling ball or blowing wind is not seen as having energy; the damage/movement evidence counters this.
Confusing energy with the force or 'push' the object carries (impetus) — the moving object HAS energy (it can do something), it does not contain a stored push that 'runs out'.
Treating speed and energy as the same thing rather than speed being the EVIDENCE for how much kinetic energy there is.
'A heavier object always has more energy' — mass matters too, but it is deliberately held constant here; don't let it smuggle in (kept for later).
'A stationary object has no energy at all' — it may have stored/potential energy; here we only claim it has no KINETIC energy.

learn.summary: For ages 9–10, help children use evidence they gather to explain that a moving object has energy (kinetic energy / energy of motion), and that the faster it moves the more energy it has. Keep it strictly qualitative and comparative ('faster → more effect, more energy'): no formulas, no ½mv², no speed or energy measurements. Build the explanation from observed effects (knocks over more, pushes farther, makes a bigger dent/louder bang) while holding the object the same so only speed varies. Name the term precisely and tie it to what children have seen, and separate 'has energy' from 'carries a push' to head off the impetus idea.

activities.title: Launch-and-hit bench: build the speed→energy explanation from your own trials
feedback: If a learner can predict the damage from the speed alone before firing, prompt them to put the rule into words and name the evidence: 'which shot had more energy, and how do you know?'

If a learner says the fast ball has 'more force' or 'more push', separate the words: the push is what acts during contact; the energy is what the moving ball carries and hands over — more speed means more energy to give.
If a learner thinks only the heavier ball matters, point out it was the SAME ball every trial, so only speed changed, yet the effect grew — so speed alone increased the energy here.

If a learner says a still ball already 'has the speed energy stored inside', note that kinetic energy exists only while moving; a still ball has none of it (though a raised ball can store another kind of energy).
activities.rationale: The NGSS performance expectation asks children to use evidence to construct the explanation, so the child should generate the evidence through controlled trials rather than just be told the rule. Holding the object constant isolates speed and quietly models fair testing while keeping mass (a later idea) out of the pattern.
sourceClaims: 4-PS3-1 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-1]'); DCI PS3.A '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-1]'; assessment boundary excludes quantitative speed measures and any precise/quantitative definition of energy.
learnerActions: Use the SAME ball every time and change only its launch speed (a slider or a fixed ramp released from a low vs high start).

Choose one target (a row of skittles, a loose block, or a sand pit), set it up the same way and in the same place for every trial, fire the ball at it, and record the outcome each trial: how many fell, how far the block moved, how big the dent.
Run several trials ordered slow → medium → fast and lay the outcomes side by side as a results strip.
After a few shots, PREDICT the result of the next speed before firing, then fire to check.
State the explanation in words and point to your evidence: 'the faster it moves, the more energy it has — I know because it knocked over more / pushed it farther.'
Say the term out loud for what the moving ball has: 'kinetic energy' or 'energy of motion'.
activities.intendedInsight: A moving object has kinetic energy; the faster it moves the more energy it has, and comparing the size of the effect on the same target is the evidence for which shot had more energy. Keeping the same object and the same target setup isolates speed as the cause.

activities.title: Swap the evidence: same rule, different effect
feedback: If a learner treats one effect (e.g. toppling) as the only sign of energy, show that distance pushed and loudness also grow with speed — all are evidence of more energy.
Reinforce naming: in each case the faster ball had more kinetic energy, shown by a bigger effect.
activities.rationale: Seeing the same qualitative rule across different outcomes supports transfer and keeps the claim about energy rather than one particular effect.
learnerActions: Repeat the fast-vs-slow comparison but change what the ball hits: a sand crater to dent, a block to shove, or a buzzer/plate that sounds louder on a harder hit.
For each target, decide which speed produced the bigger effect and say what that tells you about the energy.
Compare across targets: check whether the same rule ('faster → more energy') shows up as more damage, more distance, AND a louder bang in your own results.
activities.intendedInsight: The relationship between speed and energy is general: it shows up in many kinds of evidence, not just one toppling task, so the explanation is about the moving object's energy rather than one specific effect.

activities.title: Predict-and-check: ramp roll into dominoes (diagnostic reasoning)
feedback: A full response: more speed → more kinetic energy → more energy transferred to the dominoes (object held constant), and the child transfers the reasoning to a new case (e.g. where the energy went).
A partial response names more energy and more dominoes but can't connect it to energy TRANSFER, or slips into force or mass language — prompt gently toward 'what did the moving object hand over?'

A gap response explains only via 'more force/push' or claims a still object has kinetic energy — reteach the distinction between a contact push and carried energy, and that kinetic energy exists only while moving.
activities.rationale: Asking for the prediction AND the reason discriminates a speed→force story from a speed→energy→effect story, matching the standard's emphasis on evidence-based explanation.
sourceClaims: Children commonly attribute energy only to living/engine-driven things and confuse a moving object's energy with a 'push' it carries (impetus).
learnerActions: Roll the same object down a ramp from a low start, then from a high start (a higher start, on the same ramp, means it is moving faster at the bottom) into a row of dominoes/blocks.
BEFORE the fast roll, predict how many will move compared with the slow roll, AND say why.
Run the roll and compare your prediction with the result.
Answer the follow-ups: 'It's the same object both times — what does that let you rule out, so what's left?' and 'Where did the fast object's energy go after it hit?'
Consider a still object on the table that knocks nothing down: what does that say about whether a motionless object has kinetic energy?
activities.intendedInsight: The reason matters: a speed→energy explanation predicts more effect because faster means more energy; the sameness of the object rules out mass, leaving speed as the cause, and a motionless object has no kinetic energy.

activities.title: Name it and reference it: everyday anchors
feedback: If a learner only recognises the label but can't justify it, send them back to a trial so the word stays tied to observed effect.
Confirm correct, precise use of 'kinetic energy' or 'energy of motion' tied to a stated piece of evidence.
activities.rationale: A labelled static scene names the vocabulary and offers a frozen fast-vs-slow comparison as a reference layer; it supports naming but does not itself supply the live speed→effect evidence that drives the explanation, so it works best alongside the hands-on work. Recognising a label does not by itself show a learner can produce the explanation.
learnerActions: Point to everyday cases — a gentle vs hard kick of a football, a slow vs fast bumper car, wind turbines spinning faster in stronger wind — and say which has more energy of motion and how you can tell.
For a labelled picture of a fast cyclist, strong wind, or hard kick, reveal and read the label 'more speed → more energy of motion' to fix the vocabulary.
Use this as a reference to check your words after the hands-on trials, not as a substitute for them.
activities.intendedInsight: The term 'kinetic energy' / 'energy of motion' labels something they have observed in the world, not an abstraction detached from evidence.

constraints: Keep everything qualitative and comparative; the assessment boundary explicitly excludes measuring speed and quantifying energy at this age — no formulas or ½mv².
Hold the object (mass) constant so only speed varies; mass also affects energy but is deliberately kept for a later topic and must not smuggle into the pattern here.

Ordering trials by speed or choosing 'which knocks over more' in a recognition format can check the rule but does not, on its own, have the child GENERATE and explain the evidence; pair any recognition task with hands-on trials and a spoken/written explanation.

A labelled static picture is a vocabulary/reference scaffold: it can name kinetic energy and show a frozen comparison but cannot deliver the live speed→effect evidence, so it should support rather than lead the lesson.
Distinguish 'has energy' from 'carries a push': the moving object HAS energy it can transfer, it does not contain a stored push that runs out.
Claim only that a MOTIONLESS object has no KINETIC energy; it may still store other energy (e.g. if raised up), so avoid saying a stationary object has 'no energy at all'.

In England there is no general energy topic at KS2 (energy enters at KS3); the primary reasoning here is anchored on Working Scientifically skills, so treat this as NGSS-aligned enrichment for a UK primary setting.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source marks the NGSS/DfE claims as verified and the IOP Spark misconception claim as unverified (verified:false); treat the impetus/'only living things have energy' claim (used in the ramp-into-dominoes activity) as plausible but unconfirmed here.

Self-audit: 'a higher start means the object is moving faster at the bottom' assumes the same ramp/object and negligible added complications; this is a reasonable qualitative setup for this age and is kept as a comparative (not quantitative) claim.

Self-audit: the original correctly notes kinetic energy depends on both speed and mass; mass is intentionally held constant, so claims here are limited to 'more speed → more energy for the same object' and should not be generalised to 'faster always beats heavier'.

assess.poeTask: Roll the same object down a ramp from a low start, then from a high start (a higher start means it's moving faster at the bottom), into a row of blocks. BEFORE the second roll ask the child to predict how many blocks will move compared with the slow roll, AND why. The reason is diagnostic: a speed→energy child predicts more because faster = more energy, while a force-only or 'same object, same effect' child can't justify a difference. Then run it.
probeDeeper: It's the same marble both times. What does that let you rule out as the reason — so what's left?
Where did the fast marble's energy GO after it hit the dominoes?
Counterexample: a marble sitting still on the table knocks down no dominoes. What does that tell you about whether a still object has kinetic energy?
Would a slow bowling ball or a fast marble do more to the dominoes? What two things does the energy of motion seem to depend on?
assess.correctAnswer: The faster marble has more kinetic energy (energy of motion). The faster something moves, the more energy it carries, so it transfers more energy to the dominoes and knocks more of them down. It's the same marble, so the only difference is speed, and more speed means more energy.

errorPatterns.pattern: The fast marble has more force/push, not more energy ('it hits harder because it's got more force').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the words — force is the push during contact; energy is what the moving marble carries and hands over; more speed means more energy to give.
errorPatterns.distractor: The fast marble has more force pushing it along, and that's what knocks the dominoes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains the effect with 'force/push/power' and never uses energy, or treats force and energy as the same thing.

errorPatterns.pattern: A still object already 'has speed energy' stored inside, ready to go ('the energy is in it waiting').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Kinetic energy exists only while MOVING; a still marble has none of it, though it may store another kind of energy if it is raised up.
errorPatterns.distractor: The marble had the energy stored inside it the whole time, even before it moved.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes kinetic energy to a stationary marble.

errorPatterns.pattern: It's the heaviness that matters and speed makes no real difference ('you just need a heavier ball').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point out it's the SAME marble both times — only speed changed — so speed alone increased the effect.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ignores speed as the variable even though mass is held constant.

responseLevels.gap: Explains the effect only as 'more force/push', or says a still object has kinetic energy; doesn't link speed to energy.
responseLevels.full: Explains more speed → more kinetic energy → more energy transferred to the dominoes (holding the marble constant), and transfers the reasoning to a new case such as a bowling ball vs a marble, or where the energy went.
responseLevels.partial: Says the faster marble has more energy and knocks down more, but can't connect it to energy TRANSFER to the dominoes, or slips into force language or mass confusion.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You roll the same marble into a line of dominoes twice: once slowly, once fast. The fast marble knocks down far more dominoes. Why does the faster marble knock down more — what's different about it?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who says the fast marble has more 'force/push' but never links it to energy, or who imagines it is somehow heavier or stronger, differs from one who says more speed = more kinetic energy = more energy transferred. The reason tier separates a speed→force story from a speed→energy→effect story.
